Anatomy of a chip.
13 words from a chip design run report explained on a real 2.9 by 4.5 mm silicon die, the DG32 two domain microcontroller from Deep Grid Semi.
For every term you get the engineering meaning, the real numbers from our runs, and a plain language analogy, the chip as a city.
Think of the die as a plot of land for a new city, and the core area as the part inside the boundary wall where buildings are allowed.
The strip along the wall is kept for the gates and the utility mains.
Let's start with the two rectangles everything else lives in.
The die is the piece of silicon we get back, 2,900 by 4,500 microns, about 13 square millimeters.
Inside it, the core area is where the tools are allowed to place cells.
The 30 micron ring between them is kept for the blocks pins and power ring.
And the whole die sits inside the open frame wrapper with 133 microns of clearance on every side.
Pads are the city gates where the highways from outside arrive.
Pins are the doors on our own building that those gates connect to.
A door with nothing behind it is exactly the bug we found in September.
Pads are the metal squares a bond wire lands on.
They belong to the open frame wrapper, drawn dashed here, not to our die.
Our hardened block instead exposes pins along its edge, the small green rectangles on metal three.
The wrapper routes each of its 44 pads to the matching pin.
The reset finding of the 10th of September was exactly here. A pin existed on the edge, but the net behind it had no driver, so three and a half
thousand flops would never have come out of reset.
Macros are prefabricated buildings delivered whole, like a warehouse arriving on a truck.
Roads cannot go through them, only around them, so the width of the street between two rows of warehouses matters a great deal.
A macro is a pre-built hard block that the tool places as one object and routes around, never through.
The 16 open IMSRAMs are each 683 by 417 microns, arranged in two columns.
14 of them are the 28 kilobytes of memory. Two are the key and value buffers for the attention engine.
The 300 micron channel between the columns is the fix from run 14.
At 180 microns, the router left 25 violations it could never clear, all in one corner of bank five.
The analog converter is a delicate instrument, like a concert hall that must not have a noisy road running through it, so its wiring is marked hand
tool for every automated tool.
The SAR converter is our one analog macro, a third-party layout with its own pins, placed in the top right corner.
Its analog nets are marked don't touch, so synthesis cannot insert buffers into them.
That matters because before the 01 fix, it did exactly that, and the ADC path would never have worked.
Standard cells are the ordinary houses and shops, all built to the same height, so they line up in neat streets.
Utilization is how much of the land is built on, the rest is left free for roads.
Standard cells are the library gates, NANDs, flip-flops, buffers.
Each is one row tall, 2.72 microns.
Synthesis turns the RTL into about 105,000 of them, and placement drops them into rows between the macros.
Utilization is the fraction of the core they cover, 53% in run 15.
The rest is breathing room for wires.
Placement is city planning. Put the neighbors who talk to each other most on the same street.
The clock tree is the city's timekeeping, one bell that has to be heard everywhere at exactly the same moment.
P and R stands for place and route.
Placement decides where every cell goes, driven by timing with a density knob of 0.3 here.
Then clock tree synthesis builds the tree of buffers that carries the clock to every flop with matched delay.
This die has two clock domains, so there are two trees, the 54 MHz core clock and the fast attention clock.
Max fanout 24, the knob that closed timing on run six and seven, limits how many loads anyone buffer drives.
The power grid is the water main network with the big trunk pipes on the top floors.
Our building had put its own pipes on the very top floor, so the city's main could not pass over it.
The building had taps, but no water.
The rule is simple, leave the top floor empty for the city's mains.
The power distribution network is a grid of wide straps, metal for running vertically in violet and metal five horizontally in gold.
Here is why the CI2609 wrapper delivered no power.
Our block used metal five for its own straps, so the wrapper's metal five straps, the pale gold, could only run beside the block, never over it.
The block's VDD net had exactly one connection, itself.
The open frame convention is to cap the block at metal four and leave metal five empty, so the wrapper's straps cross over the block and via down to its metal
four pins.
That is what run 16 and the R3 met for rehardened our testing.
The metal layers are a multi-story road network.
Level one roads run east to west, level two north to south, and so on.
The higher levels are wider and faster, like motorways, but there are far fewer of them.
Sky 130 gives us five metal layers above the local interconnect.
Each has a preferred direction and a track pitch, the grid the router snaps wires onto.
Metal one runs horizontally at .34 microns, metal two vertically at .46, metal three horizontally at .68, metal four vertically at .92, and metal five
horizontally at .34 microns, wide and sparse, so it is mostly for power.
Alternating directions is why every route looks like a staircase, and it is why macro origins must sit on the metal two and metal three grid, or the router
jogs at every pin.
A via is the ramp between two levels of the road network.
Every time a wire turns a corner, it changes level, so it needs a ramp.
A via is the vertical plug that connects two adjacent layers.
Going up, McCon from local interconnect to metal one, then via, via two, via three, and via four.
Whenever a wire changes direction, it changes layer, so it needs a via.
The warning PDN 0110, no via inserted, means a metal four strap ended under a metal five strap with too little overlap to fit one.
A two had 151 of those, K layout found them harmless.
Global routing is planning the bus routes on a map of the city.
Detailed routing is actually painting the lane markings on every single street.
Routing happens in two stages.
Global routing plans every net through a coarse grid of G cells and reports overflow wherever more wires want to sell than it has tracks.
Zero overflow, as we had in run 15, means congestion is not the problem.
Detailed routing then draws the real wires on real tracks layer by layer following those guides.
In run 16, the metal five guide count is zero, which confirms the met four cap is in effect.
Each router pass is a traffic engineer walking the city and fixing every spot where two lanes touch.
The number of problems should shrink on every walk.
If it stops shrinking, the cause is one badly shaped junction, not too much traffic.
The detailed router works in passes.
Each pass rips up and reroutes wires that break a spacing or shorting rule, then reports how many violations remain.
Run 16 started at 193,000 and halved in the first pass.
Run 15 went from 175,000 to zero in 20 passes.
When the count plateaus instead, like run 12 stuck at 25 in a single 30 micron square, the cause is geometry, not congestion, and more passes will never
fix it.

Slack is the margin between how long a signal takes to cross town and the time the bell allows.
Negative slack means one particular journey is too long.
The fixes are moving the buildings closer, adding a relay station, or splitting the journey into two legs.

Positive means closed.
